newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: DUTCH GIANTS REVEAL ALL FOR WALL STREET DEBUTS.
newsitem.headline: DUTCH GIANTS REVEAL ALL FOR WALL STREET DEBUTS.

text.p: ABN AMRO and ING Groep will continue their remarkably similar developments when their shares list in New York over the next month.

Analysts said the U.S. share market debuts of the two biggest financial institutions in the Netherlands underlined their appetite for expansion in the United States and heralded further acquisitions in the world's biggest economy.
But the timing of the events was related more to their recent decision to reveal the size of hidden reserves, prompted by changes in European Union banking regulations.
"Now there's really nothing to hide any more," a banking analyst said recently.
ABN AMRO, the largest bank in the Netherlands, earlier this month issued a prospectus for a small capital raising which is accompanying its listing on Wednesday.
The document, more detailed than the bank had provided in the past because it had to meet stringent U.S. GAAP accounting rules, contained few surprises, analysts said.
They are looking forward more to ING's prospectus because it will detail previously-undisclosed gains on the group's huge investment portfolio.
The ING document is being issued ahead of its planned listing on June 12.
ABN AMRO and ING were both formed through mergers in the early 1990s, and the small size of their home market has forced them to expand offshore, including into the U.S. market.
ABN AMRO is one of the biggest foreign banks in the United States, where it has built a beach-head in the mid-west, while ING is a major player in the U.S. insurance industry.
ING is interested in buying a large U.S. life insurer to give itself the critical mass to compete against big foreign insurers, including Dutch rival Aegon .

It is also keen to expand its securities distribution business in the United States, having pulled out of talks last week to buy Wall Street investment bank Dillon Read & Co, which was then sold to SBC Warburg.

Analysts believe ING is more likely to make the next big U.S. takeover rather than ABN AMRO, which is still digesting Michigan-based Standard Federal Bank Inc, bought in a $1.9 billion deal completed earlier this month.
Analysts said both companies had increased the efficiency of their domestic operations through post-merger cost cutting but needed acquisitions to maintain the momentum in earnings growth.
"Everything is on track and successful. It's natural that you look abroad more," said ING Barings analyst Daan Worm.
He said both groups also wanted to broaden their shareholder base, and a Wall Street listing would expose them to U.S. pension funds which can only invest in U.S. listed companies.
U.S. investors hold only nine percent of ABN AMRO shares while U.S. and Canadian investors hold 13 percent of ING.
Hans Pluigjers of Kempen and Co said a New York listing would allow also both companies to make acquisitions in the United States using their own shares as a payment method.

Until now, ING and ABN AMRO have been forced to make cash-only takeovers because only U.S.-listed shares may be used in U.S. acquisitions. "Sellers are more interested if you use shares because there's no tax liability on them," he said.

BZW analyst Heinie Hakker said the two Dutch groups were prepared to list in New York because they were more comfortable about complying with U.S. GAAP accounting standards, which require greater financial disclosure than Dutch rules.
The key element was the decision by both groups earlier this year to reveal the size of their previously hidden reserves to comply with changes to European Union regulations.
The reserves, built up over time as the banks overprovided for loan losses, amounted to 4.02 billion guilders for ABN AMRO and 2.55 billion guilders for ING, both at December 31.
"It was always an obstacle. They were rather secretive about that," Hakker said.
The ABN AMRO prospectus included the first time breakdown of divisional profits and revealed that doubtful loans fell in the last two years although the balance sheet continued to grow.
"That's one of the reasons why everybody is buying Dutch banks ... because the quality of the loan portfolio is extremely healthy," said Bart van der Feen of IRIS.

He said ING could afford to spend seven to eight billion guilders on an acquisition, although it was unlikely to do so in one deal. "I am expecting a very big acquisition in the U.S. life (insurance) market before the end of the year," he added.
ING missed out on an opportunity last year when it tried to buy U.S. insurer First Colony, later sold to GE Capital .
Analysts said ING's financial muscle stemmed partly from the gains on its 188 billion guilder investment portfolio.
Under U.S. GAAP accounting principles, ING will have to restate profits to include realised gains on its investment portfolio, a practice not required under Dutch rules. @
Pluijgers estimates them at 982 million guilders in 1996, compared with the 499 million guilders revealed by ABN AMRO.

Analysts have said the ING prospectus will make comparisons with Aegon and other European insurers easier, underline the group's strength and confirm the positive effect on profits of a new system of risk provisioning.
From this year, both groups will deduct only actual loan losses from profits, giving them a one-off boost in profits.
